summary: This standards-track RFC defines the MRT Lowpoint algorithm used in the Default MRT Profile. It computes the maximally redundant trees and their next hops for the fast reroute approach in RFC 7812.

eli5.summary: If a road is blocked, you need a backup route ready. This is the exact recipe for working out the two separate backup routes.

questions: how are maximally redundant trees computed
what is the mrt lowpoint algorithm
how does mrt fast reroute pick an alternate
subtitle: The exact recipe routers use to compute two separate backup routes to every destination, so a single failure can be survived.

tldr.problem: A router that loses a link or neighbor needs a backup next hop chosen in advance, and every router in the area must compute the backup trees in a consistent way.
tldr.mechanism: The MRT Lowpoint algorithm builds one common graph (a GADAG) using depth-first search and lowpoint values, then derives MRT-Blue and MRT-Red next hops from it and picks whichever one avoids the failed primary next hop.
tldr.outcome: Used with RFC 7812, it guarantees 100% recovery for single failures when the network is 2-connected, regardless of link metrics. It is required when the Default MRT Profile is implemented.

facts.label: Guarantee
facts.value: 100% recovery for single failures in a 2-connected network

today: RFC 7811 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2016 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It is the algorithm companion to the architecture in RFC 7812.

sections.title: What the Algorithm Computes
sections.content:
MRT Fast Reroute needs packets to be forwardable not only along the shortest-path tree but also along two Maximally Redundant Trees, called MRT-Blue and MRT-Red. A router that sees a local failure must also have decided in advance which alternate to use. This RFC defines how to compute those three things for the architecture in RFC 7812.

Used for MRT Fast-Reroute, the algorithm guarantees 100% recovery for single failures when the network is 2-connected, and that guarantee does not depend on the link metrics an operator uses for traffic engineering. It also handles graphs that are not 2-connected. Each MRT is a spanning tree, and the two give each node two paths to the root that share the minimum number of nodes and links. Any shared node is a cut-vertex and any shared link is a cut-link.

Because packets are routed hop by hop, every router must compute the MRT-Blue and MRT-Red next hops consistently, just as with shortest-path trees. A router's forwarding table then holds primary next hops for the shortest-path tree, for MRT-Blue and for MRT-Red.
sections.eli5: Picture two roads from your house to the town square that share as few stretches as possible. If one is closed, you take the other, and everyone in town agrees how the two roads are drawn.

sections.title: Partial Order, Ears and the GADAG
sections.content:
The core idea is to partially order the nodes. A directed link from X to Y means X is lower in the order (X<<Y). The root R is placed at both the very bottom and the very top. From any node you can climb to higher nodes until you reach R, or step down to lower ones until you reach R, and these increasing and decreasing paths cannot share nodes. Such a graph is called an Almost DAG (ADAG), because removing the links directed to the root would leave a DAG. For graphs with several blocks, the result is a Generalized ADAG (GADAG).

An ADAG is built by finding a cycle through the root and then repeatedly adding an ear: a path whose two ends are already in the graph and whose other nodes are not. If one end is lower than the other, the ear is directed from lower to higher so that no cycle forms. If the ends are unordered, either direction works. If one end is the root, the ear is directed so that the root is the lower end.
sections.eli5: Imagine lining up kids by height, with the teacher standing at both ends of the line. You can walk up the line or down the line to reach the teacher, and the two walks never bump into each other.

sections.title: Lowpoint Values, Blocks and Local Roots
sections.content:
The algorithm runs a depth-first search (DFS) and numbers nodes with D(x). The lowpoint L(x) is the smallest DFS number reachable from x or its descendants by one back-edge, computed as the minimum of D(x), the lowest D over back-edges, and the lowest L over tree-edge children. If a child c has L(c) >= D(x), then x is a cut-vertex.

A graph that is not 2-connected is made of blocks: 2-connected clusters, cut-links or isolated nodes. The RFC's example graph has four blocks, three clusters and one cut-link. Each node gets a localroot, the cut-vertex (or root) in its block that is closest to the root, and a Block-ID. Two nodes share a block if they have the same localroot, or one is the other's localroot. Redundant trees are built in each block and then combined; a cut-link is added in the same direction to both trees.
sections.eli5: If a map has a bridge that every trip must cross, the bridge is a weak spot. The algorithm finds those weak spots by tracking how far back each town can reach without using the road it arrived by.

sections.title: Building the GADAG
sections.content:
Every router MUST order its interfaces identically: by metric, then by the neighbor's mrt_node_id, both compared as unsigned integers. Without this, different routers could explore ears in different orders and build different GADAGs. All routers in the MRT Island MUST also select the same GADAG root, using the Default MRT Profile's selection policy, and interfaces start out marked UNDIRECTED.

The Lowpoint Inheritance method then finds ears from a node already in the GADAG in two ways: via a DFS child, following lowpoint parents, or via a non-DFS-child neighbor, following DFS parents. Ears are kept on a stack so earlier nodes are processed in the right order, and localroots are inherited from the end of the ear.

Links not yet directed are then given a direction. A topological sort (Kahn's method) gives a total order consistent with the GADAG, and remaining UNDIRECTED links are directed from lower to higher. Links from a block root get special handling, and a cut-link ends up directed both INCOMING and OUTGOING.
sections.eli5: Everybody has to number the roads the same way and pick the same starting square. Then every router, working alone, draws the exact same map.

sections.title: Computing MRT-Blue and MRT-Red Next Hops
sections.content:
One GADAG serves all destinations. A router X runs an increasing SPF along OUTGOING links and a decreasing SPF along INCOMING links, without exploring links from the root (or from X's localroot). Increasing next hops to nodes higher than X are X's MRT-Blue next hops, and decreasing next hops to nodes lower than X are its MRT-Red next hops. For a destination Y higher than X, the MRT-Red next hop is the one used to reach the root, and for Y lower than X, the MRT-Blue next hop is the one used to reach the root.

For a destination Y that is unordered with X, the Blue path decreases to a node H lower than Y and then increases, while the Red path increases to a node G higher than Y and then decreases. They are node-disjoint because G and H cannot be the same node. For destinations in other blocks, next hops are inherited through the relevant cut-vertex, recorded as an order_proxy.

An implementation MAY choose any subset of these next hops that stays within the allowed interval toward the destination, and SHOULD implement Select_Alternates() to pick an MRT-FRR alternate.
sections.eli5: Each router walks up the line and down the line to find the first step of each of the two routes. It never has to know the whole route, only which way to take the first step.

sections.title: Choosing the Alternate
sections.content:
For each primary next-hop node F toward a destination D, the computing router S must decide whether MRT-Blue or MRT-Red avoids F. Select_Alternates() compares where D and F sit relative to S in the partial order, and uses topological order values when needed, then returns USE_BLUE, USE_RED or USE_RED_OR_BLUE.

If F is D itself, or F is the order proxy for D, only link protection is possible. The MRT that does not use the failed primary next hop is used. If both use it, the link is a cut-link, and the MRT next hops must be pruned to avoid the failed interface. The RFC explains each other case in a table by deducing whether F lies on an increasing path, a decreasing path or neither, then picking the color that avoids it. One tricky case relies on the way these GADAGs are built: incoming links to a localroot come from only one other node in the same block.

The RFC notes that other alternates, such as downstream Loop-Free Alternates, may be preferred when available.
sections.eli5: When the road to town is blocked, the router asks which of its two backup routes does not go through the blocked spot, and takes that one.

sections.title: Proxy-Nodes and Broadcast Networks
sections.content:
A named proxy-node stands for something outside the MRT Island, such as a prefix. Each is attached to two proxy-node attachment routers, chosen as the two lowest named-proxy-cost candidates, with ties broken by lowest Router ID. Candidates are routers in the island that advertise the prefix, and Island Border Router and Island Neighbor pairs where the neighbor's shortest path to the prefix does not enter the island. All routers MUST reach the same conclusion on which neighbors are loop-free, so they MUST use a result identical to the specified Island_Marking_SPF().

On broadcast networks, a pseudonode represents the network, with a non-zero metric from each real node to it and zero in the other direction. Pseudonodes MUST be included when computing the GADAG but MUST NOT be GADAG root candidates, which keeps the root stable when the Designated Router changes. A router attached to a pseudonode MUST also run the algorithm from the point of view of each pseudonode neighbor, so it can find a real next hop on the broadcast network.
sections.eli5: Some places are not on the map of routers, and a shared hallway counts as a place of its own. The routers pretend these stand-in places are real so the two routes still work.

sections.title: Operations, Evaluation and Security
sections.content:
It is RECOMMENDED that operators give lower (more preferred) GADAG Root Selection Priority values to routers that are central and expected to stay in the IGP topology. The RFC says centrality can significantly affect alternate path lengths, and a changed root can change the Blue and Red forwarding entries.

The RFC compared three ways of building a GADAG on five service provider topologies. The Lowpoint method was chosen because it needs the least computation. Two of the five topologies (T216 and T219) showed noticeably shorter alternates with the SPF-based method, so other variants may be worth specifying later. A GADAG rooted at each destination is also possible but would need a new MRT profile.

The algorithm introduces no new security concerns beyond those in RFC 7812.
sections.eli5: Pick the starting square in the middle of town, and one that is unlikely to vanish. The shorter the routes, the sooner everyone gets home.

items.title: Where is D?
items.text: Higher than S, lower than S, or unordered with S.

items.title: Where is F?
items.text: The failed primary next hop is compared with S in the same way.

items.title: Topological order
items.text: Used to compare F with D when both sit on the same side of S.
